transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I can’t seem to keep my work straight anymore—projects, emails, and deadlines keep getting jumbled and I feel like I’ve lost my ability to stay organized. I recently transitioned into a much more demanding administrative role, and my manager suggested I talk to a professional because I've been feeling so scattered and overwhelmed. I'm just really worried because I've always been the dependable, organized one, and now I feel like I'm completely slipping.
Have you been experiencing excessive worry or fear about your performance or the future since you started feeling overwhelmed with your new role?

Yes, I've been feeling so anxious and alarmed about it. I am absolutely terrified that I'll lose my recent promotion and my reputation as the dependable, organized person in the office. It's gotten to the point where I'm up late panicking because I've avoided and pushed off major tasks during the day.

Can you tell me more about what you think triggered this feeling of being overwhelmed and disorganized - was it specifically the new job role, or was there something else that happened around the same time that might have contributed to how you're feeling?

It was really a combination of several major changes that hit all at once about a year and three months ago. Along with the company reorganization and my promotion to a much more demanding role, my spouse and I were adjusting to a recent move, and I had taken on extra church and community commitments. All of these cumulative demands piling up at the same time just completely pushed me past what my usual organizing systems could handle.

You mentioned that these changes occurred about a year and three months ago, can you tell me if your feelings of being overwhelmed, anxious, and disorganized have been constant since then or have they worsened over time?

They have actually been consistently severe and overwhelming ever since everything changed a year and three months ago. The problems spiraled very quickly back then, and they've stayed at this same high, difficult level ever since rather than gradually getting worse over time.

Have you experienced any significant reduction in your symptoms or return to your normal level of functioning during any periods where the stress or demands from your job, move, or other commitments were temporarily reduced or absent?

To be honest, I haven't really had any periods where the demands from my job, our move, or my commitments have let up since everything started a year and three months ago. Because it's been non-stop, I'm really not sure if my symptoms would improve if I actually got a break.

If you were to take a break from your current responsibilities and commitments for an extended period, do you think your feelings of being overwhelmed, anxious, and disorganized would significantly improve, or do you believe they would persist?

I'm not really sure, honestly, because I haven't had the chance to take a real break since all of this started. I haven't thought much about whether a break would completely solve the problem or if it would just temporarily relieve the pressure.

Do you think your anxiety and feelings of being overwhelmed are primarily focused on your work performance and the demands of your new role, or are they more generalized and also affecting other areas of your life, such as your relationships or daily activities?

It has definitely spilled over into my personal life, not just work. I’m constantly dropping the ball at home by forgetting grocery lists, missing dentist appointments, and even paying bills late, which is causing a lot of tension with my spouse. I'm also really struggling to keep up with my church and community commitments because of it.
You mentioned avoiding and pushing off major tasks during the day, can you tell me more about what specifically happens when you try to start or work on these tasks that makes you avoid them?

Whenever I try to sit and focus on a big task, like reviewing contract changes or reading long emails, I feel this mental wall go up. I'll find any excuse to avoid it, like checking my phone, getting coffee, or suddenly deciding to file papers instead. Those major tasks just keep getting pushed off until I'm up late at night panicking about them.
When you avoid these tasks, is it primarily because you're worried about not doing them perfectly, or is it more about feeling overwhelmed by the task itself and not knowing where to start?

It’s definitely more about feeling overwhelmed and hitting that mental wall rather than trying to be perfect. When I sit down to tackle those big tasks, I struggle to figure out where to start or how to prioritize them. I'll try to organize my day and end up with three different to-do lists and Post-its everywhere, completely unable to tell what I should actually do first.
Can you describe a specific instance where you successfully completed a task despite feeling overwhelmed, and what helped you to overcome your avoidance and get it done?

Honestly, I really struggle to find anything that actually helps me overcome that avoidance lately, and I don't have a healthy way of getting past that mental wall. The only way those big tasks get done now is when sheer panic sets in at the absolute last minute, forcing me to stay up late to finish them. My old coping systems, like checklists and color-coding, just don't seem to work for these larger projects anymore.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms, such as tremors, palpitations, or sweating, when you're faced with tasks that trigger your avoidance behavior?

No, I don't really experience physical symptoms like tremors, sweating, or heart palpitations when I'm avoiding things. Instead, it's more of a strong mental block where my brain just shuts down, or I feel this general restlessness that makes it hard to sit still.

Do you feel that your mental block and avoidance of tasks are primarily due to the excessive demands and pressures of your current situation, or do you think there's something more fundamentally changed in your ability to cope with stress and manage your daily life?

I think it’s a combination of both. The sudden increase in demands over the last 15 months has completely overwhelmed the coping mechanisms, like color-coding and staying late, that I always relied on to manage. However, this isn't entirely new; I've actually struggled with focus and daydreaming since childhood, but I'm just no longer able to compensate for those underlying issues under this much stress.

Do you believe that if the external stressors, such as the demands of your new role and other commitments, were significantly reduced or managed, your underlying issues with focus and daydreaming would still cause you significant distress and impairment in your daily life?

Yes, I do believe they would still cause me distress, because even before this promotion, I had to work twice as hard as everyone else and stay late just to mask how much I struggled. These issues actually go all the way back to my childhood, where my teachers noted I daydreamed and my mom had to walk me through everything step-by-step. Even without the recent stress, managing my focus and organization has always required an exhausting amount of extra effort.
Can you describe how your difficulties with focus and daydreaming have impacted your daily life and relationships over the years, separate from the recent stress and demands of your new role?

Looking back, these struggles go all the way back to my childhood. In elementary school, my teachers always wrote on report cards that I was bright but daydreamed and forgot instructions, and my mom got so frustrated because I'd lose my homework or forget chores unless she guided me step-by-step.

Did your difficulties with focus, daydreaming, and organization exist prior to the age of 12, and have they been persistent throughout your life, or did they start later in your childhood or adolescence?

Yes, they absolutely existed before I was 12. Looking back at elementary school, my teachers frequently wrote on my report cards that I was bright but daydreamed and forgot instructions. My mom also used to get so frustrated with me because I would constantly lose my homework sheets or forget what she asked me to do unless she stood there and walked me through it step-by-step.

Can you confirm that your symptoms of inattention, disorganization, and daydreaming have been present and caused you significant difficulties since childhood, and not just a recent development in response to the increased stress and demands of your new role?

Yes, I can absolutely confirm that these struggles go all the way back to my childhood and aren't just a recent development. Even in elementary school, my teachers wrote that I daydreamed and forgot instructions, and my mom had to guide me step-by-step because I'd constantly lose my homework. The recent promotion and stress just made it impossible to hide anymore, but the underlying pattern has always been there.

Have you also experienced symptoms of restlessness, fidgeting, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, alongside your difficulties with focus and organization, either currently or during your childhood?

Lately, I do feel very restless in meetings and catch myself constantly bouncing my leg, clicking pens, or even needing to get up and walk around just to get out of my chair. However, as a child, I didn't really have that physical hyperactivity; my struggles back then were much more about daydreaming, losing things, and forgetting instructions.

Can you describe if this restlessness and fidgeting you're experiencing now is a new development, or if you also had similar symptoms of hyperactivity during your childhood, alongside your difficulties with focus and organization?

The physical restlessness, like bouncing my leg and needing to get up during meetings, is definitely a newer development that has gotten worse under my current stress. In contrast, I didn't experience any of that physical hyperactivity as a child. Back then, my struggles were strictly focused on daydreaming, forgetting instructions, losing my homework, and needing step-by-step guidance.
Can you estimate how long you've been experiencing this restlessness and fidgeting, and if it's directly related to the stress of your new role or if it seems to be a separate issue?

This severe restlessness and fidgeting started about a year and three months ago, right around the time of my promotion and our move. While I might have had minor habits before, the constant leg bouncing and needing to get up during meetings really spiraled into a major issue under the pressure and stress of my new responsibilities.

Have you experienced any significant symptoms of hyperactivity, such as talking excessively, interrupting others, or feeling constantly 'on the go,' either as a child or in your current state, beyond the restlessness and fidgeting you've described?

No, I don't really experience those specific symptoms like talking excessively, interrupting others, or feeling constantly "on the go." My struggles have always been much more about trying to keep my thoughts and tasks organized rather than being overly active in those ways.

Do you think your difficulties with focus, organization, and restlessness would significantly improve if you found ways to better manage your stress and anxiety, or do you believe these issues are more intrinsic to your functioning and would persist regardless of your stress levels?

I believe these issues are intrinsic and would persist, even though the recent stress has made them much worse. Even before my promotion, I had to work unusually hard to stay organized, relying on intense color-coded calendars and staying late just to keep track of details. These struggles go all the way back to my childhood, where I frequently lost my homework and my teachers noted that I daydreamed and forgot instructions.
If you were able to effectively manage your stress and anxiety, do you think you would still struggle with focus, organization, and restlessness, or would these issues significantly improve?

Yes, I believe I would still struggle because these issues go all the way back to my childhood, long before my current adult stressors. Even before this stressful promotion, I had to put an exhausting amount of extra effort and rely on strict organizing systems just to keep my head above water.
Can you think of any situations where you were able to focus and complete tasks without significant difficulty, and if so, what made those situations different from your current challenges?

Before my promotion and move about 15 months ago, I was actually known as the "organized one" at work because I managed to get things done. I only achieved that by relying heavily on color-coded calendars, checklists, and staying late to compensate for the extra effort it took me to stay on track. Now, the sheer volume and complexity of my new responsibilities have completely overwhelmed those coping mechanisms, making it impossible to keep up.

Have you experienced any symptoms of hyperactivity, such as feeling constantly 'on the go' or having difficulty engaging in leisure activities quietly, consistently over the past year, or have these symptoms been episodic and related to specific stressors?

While I don't feel constantly "on the go" in a high-energy way, I definitely experience persistent physical restlessness, like constantly bouncing my leg, clicking pens, and having a hard time staying seated in meetings or at church. These symptoms haven't been short, isolated episodes; they have been consistent and have really spiraled over the past year and three months since my company's reorganization.

You've mentioned that your difficulties with focus, organization, and restlessness have been present since childhood, but have worsened over the past year with increased stress. Can you clarify if the worsening of these symptoms over the past year is primarily due to the increased stress and demands of your new role, or if you believe there's an underlying condition that's contributing to these struggles?

It really feels like a combination of both. While the massive increase in demands from my promotion and move triggered this sudden breakdown in my ability to cope, I now realize there has likely been an underlying struggle all along. Looking back at my childhood report cards and how I always had to use extreme effort and color-coded lists just to get by, the attention issues have always been there under the surface.

Have you consistently exhibited symptoms of hyperactivity, such as feeling restless or having difficulty engaging in quiet leisure activities, for at least 6 months, or have these symptoms been more episodic?

Yes, these symptoms of restlessness—like constantly bouncing my leg, fidgeting, and feeling the urge to get up during meetings or church—have been a consistent, daily struggle rather than something that comes and goes. This has been going on continuously for about a year and three months now, ever since my company reorganized and I took on this new role.

Can you confirm that your symptoms of inattention and disorganization have been present since childhood and have persisted into adulthood, rather than starting recently in response to stress or other factors?

Yes, I can absolutely confirm that. While these issues have spiraled and become completely unmanageable over the last year and three months since my promotion and move, they actually date back to my childhood. Even back in elementary school, my report cards noted I was "bright but daydreams and forgets instructions," and my mother would get so frustrated with me losing homework or forgetting tasks unless she guided me step-by-step.

Have you ever been diagnosed with or suspected of having Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) by a healthcare professional, given your long-standing struggles with focus, organization, and recent symptoms of restlessness?

No, I have never been formally diagnosed with ADHD before, and this evaluation is actually my first time seeking professional help. My manager recently suggested I speak to someone about my stress and possible attention issues after noticing how scattered I've been. Looking back, even though my mom and teachers noticed my daydreaming and struggle with instructions as a child, it was never formally evaluated or diagnosed back then.

Can you describe any times when you felt like you were able to focus and avoid distractions without much effort, and if so, what was different about those situations compared to your current challenges?

To be honest, there has never really been a time in my life when focusing came without much effort. Even when I was successful and known as the "organized one" in my previous role, it actually required an immense amount of work behind the scenes with color-coded calendars, checklists, and staying late just to keep track of details. The only difference now is that with the massive demands of my new promotion and move, those coping mechanisms are no longer enough to keep me afloat.

If you were to receive treatment for your current stress and anxiety, do you think your underlying difficulties with focus, organization, and restlessness would still be present, or would they significantly improve?

I'm not entirely sure how much of it is just the current stress versus something that has always been there. I've had some of these struggles since childhood, but they've only recently become completely unmanageable. I suspect the core focus and organization issues would still be there even if my stress and anxiety were treated.
